{{< include _setup.qmd >}}

The rest of this site reports what the data supports. This page is the other list:
the questions we know are open. None of them changes what is reported here today,
and none of them is a commitment to do the work.

They fall into four kinds, and the first kind is not like the other three: those
questions could change what is already published, while the rest would extend it.

## Is the answer right?

### 1. Are too many samples called pristine?

The pristine verdict is a set of thresholds, and the concentration thresholds are
cut from the offshore data itself. Offshore is not the same as clean. If the
reference already carries a regional signal then the bar sits too low and the
pristine share flatters the seabed. Nothing here tests the verdict against a
baseline that was derived some other way. See
[Estimation of Pristine Sediment](methods-pristine.qmd).

### 2. Is the background the same in 1975 as it is today?

The measurements span half a century, and the background is estimated as one
number per element and fraction across all of it. If the natural level itself
moved over that time, an old sample and a recent one are being judged against
different truths, and it is not obvious which way the error would run. Nothing
here has tested whether it moved, and the temporal work that does exist was built
to answer a different question on a different database.

### 3. How confident is a verdict near the threshold?

A sample just inside a threshold is called pristine and one just outside it is not,
with nothing said about which side the measurement uncertainty would put it on.
Reporting a probability rather than a yes or no would be more honest about the
marginal cases, and would let the maps show the clear results apart from the
close ones.

## What the database already holds and does not use

Three questions that need no new sampling. The measurements exist; what is missing
is a way to get an answer out of them.

### 4. Can the values below the detection limit be recovered?

Molybdenum and selenium have no verdict because most of their measurements fell
below the limit of quantification, and those rows are deleted during cleaning. That
is right for finding contamination and wrong for finding a background, because it
deletes exactly the low end a background is made of. Statistics for left-censored
data exist for this situation and are routine elsewhere in environmental chemistry.
If one of them works here, two of the seven elements move from having no answer to
having one. See [Molybdenum](element-mo.qmd) and [Selenium](element-se.qmd).

### 5. Can the repeat visits be used for more?

Many places have been sampled more than once, and the database groups those
repeats. So far they are used only to describe where repeat-sampled places are,
which mattered because they turn out to sit close to fish farms. They could also
give something the background estimates currently lack: a measure of how much two
visits to the same place disagree, which is the floor under any claim that two
places differ.

### 6. Can the layers of a multicorer be used?

A multicorer brings up several layers from one spot, and the deeper layers were
laid down before most industrial input. The database records the depth of the
layers and the merged analyses look at them, but the background here is still
estimated across space rather than down a core. A local pre-industrial layer would
be a different kind of reference, and possibly a better one, because it controls
for place exactly rather than statistically.

## Judging more of the seabed, and judging it more fairly

Most of the seabed cannot be judged at all, and some of what can be judged is
measured against a reference that does not resemble it. These four are different
routes at that same wall, and only one of them has to work.

### 7. Is aluminium the only possible normaliser?

Aluminium is the only normaliser a verdict is allowed to use, and iron is
deliberately excluded because Norwegian fish feed contains it. Lithium, scandium,
titanium and caesium are the usual alternatives in the sediment literature, and
four of the five sources did measure at least one of them, lithium at close to the
scale of aluminium itself.

That much has now been checked, and it does not lead where it looked as though it
might. Lithium is measured on very nearly the same samples aluminium is, so putting
it in aluminium's place would add almost no new ground. What cannot be judged today
is mostly data from a source that measured no normaliser of any kind, and there is
nothing there to stand in. An alternative could still be worth having where the two
disagree, and whether any of them is confounded by fish farming the way iron is
would have to be settled before one could be used, but this is now the least
promising of the four routes rather than the most.

### 8. Can a clean location count for more than one element?

Each element is judged on its own, and a place that is pristine for copper is not
automatically pristine for zinc. But most of what stops an element being judged is
a missing normaliser rather than a missing measurement, so a location that comes
out clean where the data are good might stand in where they are not. Whether that
is a fair inference or a circular one is not settled. This is the largest of the
open questions, because it is the one that would close the coverage gap described
under [The verdict, and its cost](methods-pristine.qmd#the-verdict-and-its-cost).

### 9. Does interpolation work for some elements?

The maps draw cells that hold data and leave the space between them blank. Where
sampling is dense and the chemistry varies smoothly, filling that space would give
a continuous surface instead of a scatter of cells. Where it is sparse it would
invent detail that was never measured. Which elements, if any, are dense enough is
an open question; only copper and zinc have anything like the coverage it would
need.

### 10. Should the sieved fractions be grouped by region first?

The sieved samples are judged against a single offshore reference, and that
reference sits largely in the southern North Sea rather than in Norwegian waters.
Grouping them by region before setting a background would compare each sample with
sediment it resembles. The cost is a smaller reference behind every group, and
below some size a regional background is worse than a distant one.

## Working with the data

### 11. Should there be a way to enter new data by hand?

Everything here is rebuilt from five external exports, and a rebuild overwrites
whatever was there before. There is no form for adding a measurement and no
validation path for one. Whether the project should accept direct entry at all,
and where it would live if it did, has not been decided.
